note: Qualitative agronomy rules only: no yields, prices or water volumes are stated. Every rule lists the source(s) it comes from. 'climates' says where a rule is used: 'cool' rules only in places under the cool-climate threshold, 'warm' rules everywhere else (a 'warm' tag means no source was found supporting the rule for cool places; the threshold itself is set in code, see docs/methodology.md). Sources were checked on 2026-11-14; re-check wording before publishing.

fao_sorghum.citation: FAO Land & Water, Crop information: Sorghum
fao_sorghum.supports: Sorghum is described as relatively more drought-resistant than many other crops, e.g. maize.

hadebe_sorghum.citation: Hadebe, Modi & Mabhaudhi. Drought Tolerance and Water Use of Cereal Crops: A Focus on Sorghum as a Food Security Crop in Sub-Saharan Africa (record in FAO AGRIS)
hadebe_sorghum.supports: Sorghum has high and stable water-use efficiency and drought and heat tolerance; suggested for water-scarce arid and semi-arid zones.

un_millets.citation: UN News, Millets prove tasty solution to climate and food security challenges
un_millets.supports: Millets can grow under drought and non-irrigated conditions and have a low water footprint compared with wheat, rice or maize.

preventionweb_drought_crops.citation: PreventionWeb news article on drought-tolerant crops and methods (lists cowpea and chickpea). Author, title and date were not captured in the source check: add them before publishing
preventionweb_drought_crops.supports: Cowpea and chickpea are described as drought-tolerant grain legumes.

sare_building_soils.citation: SARE, Building Soils for Better Crops, Ch. 10 Cover Crops (Magdoff & van Es)
sare_building_soils.supports: Legume cover crops (e.g. hairy vetch, red clover) fix nitrogen with Rhizobium bacteria; cover crops enhance soil health in several ways.

sare_mcp_fertility.citation: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, Building Soil Fertility (Sarrantonio)
sare_mcp_fertility.supports: Cover crops catch nutrients before they leach; legumes add nitrogen to the soil.

nrcs_340.citation: USDA NRCS, Conservation Practice Standard: Cover Crop (Code 340)
nrcs_340.supports: Cover crops are grasses, legumes and forbs planted for seasonal vegetative cover to protect and improve soil; the standard also covers planning termination to prepare the field for the next crop and to optimise soil moisture.

sita_legumes_heat_2017.citation: Sita, K. et al. Food Legumes and Rising Temperatures: Effects, Adaptive Functional Mechanisms Specific to Reproductive Growth Stage and Strategies to Improve Heat Tolerance. Frontiers in Plant Science 8:1658 (2017)
sita_legumes_heat_2017.supports: Cool-season food legumes include broad bean, lentil, dry pea and chickpea; warm-season food legumes include pigeonpea, cowpea, mungbean and common bean, which are mainly grown in hot and humid conditions.

fao_nri_sorghum.citation: Natural Resources Institute; edited by D. Mejia and B. Lewis (FAO AGSI). SORGHUM: Post-harvest Operations. FAO Post-harvest Compendium
fao_nri_sorghum.supports: Grain sorghums are generally grown in regions which are too dry or too hot for successful maize production; sorghum is a main food grain in the semi-arid tropics.

defra_landuse_2026.citation: Defra, Agricultural land use in England at 1 June 2026 (official statistics, updated 24 September 2026)
defra_landuse_2026.supports: Wheat, winter barley, spring barley, oats, oilseed rape and field beans are reported as arable crops grown in England.

ahdb_harvest_2026.citation: AHDB, Final harvest report confirms cereal yields are below historic averages across the UK (press release, 25 September 2026)
ahdb_harvest_2026.supports: In a season shaped by limited rainfall from spring onwards, oilseed rape was the standout performer, spring barley was one of the most challenging crops and oats were below average.

ahdb_crop_ratings_2026.citation: AHDB, Crop ratings slip after dry spring, but harvest hope remains (29 June 2026)
ahdb_crop_ratings_2026.supports: Dry conditions through April and May took a toll on crop development, particularly for spring crops; spring crops faced the greatest challenges, with establishment affected by dry seedbeds.

nmsu_a129.citation: Flynn, R. and Idowu, J. Nitrogen Fixation by Legumes. New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension, Guide A-129 (revised June 2015)
nmsu_a129.supports: Alfalfa, sweet clover, true clovers, vetches, beans, peanuts, soybeans, cowpeas and fava beans are named as nitrogen-fixing legumes.

foodfoundation_beans_2026.citation: The Food Foundation, Unlocking the potential of bean, pulse and legume cultivation in the UK (briefing, July 2026)
foodfoundation_beans_2026.supports: Faba beans are otherwise known as field beans or broad beans; UK pulse production is dominated by faba beans and peas; pulses include lentils, peas, chickpeas, dry beans and faba beans; clover and sainfoin are named as legumes.

ahdb_pulses_2026.citation: Lowth, H. (AHDB). Finger on the pulse: The truth about peas, beans and other legumes (AHDB news, 19 August 2026)
ahdb_pulses_2026.supports: It's recommended to leave at least five years between pulse crops, to reduce rotational risks such as soilborne diseases.

sare_mccp_cereal_rye.citation: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd edition (2007), Nonlegume Cover Crops: Cereal Rye
sare_mccp_cereal_rye.supports: Rye is the hardiest of cereals and the best cool-season cereal cover for absorbing unused soil nitrogen (a nutrient catch crop).

uw_alfalfa_autotoxicity.citation: Jennings, J. Understanding autotoxicity in alfalfa. University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension, Crops & Soils
uw_alfalfa_autotoxicity.supports: Alfalfa can remain productive in stands from four to ten years or more; reseeding alfalfa immediately following alfalfa is not recommended in most states due to autotoxicity, seedling disease and insect pests; rotation intervals of at least 12 months have been effective in avoiding autotoxic effects.

lower_water_rules.statement: Sorghum is a drought-resistant cereal that can replace or alternate with a more water-demanding cereal.
Millets tolerate drought and have a low water footprint compared with wheat and maize.
Cowpea and chickpea are drought-tolerant grain legumes that can be added to a rotation.
lower_water_rules.order_note: Cowpea is listed first because it is a warm-season legume, while chickpea is a cool-season legume (Sita et al., 2017); these rules are used in warm places only.

lower_water_rules.statement: Oilseed rape, field beans, oats, spring barley and winter wheat are established arable crops in England, so they suit a cool-climate rotation.
lower_water_rules.order_note: Oilseed rape is listed first because it did best in the dry 2026 season; spring-sown crops are listed last because they struggled most (CL-2).

lower_water_rules.statement: In the dry 2026 UK season spring crops faced the greatest challenges: spring barley was one of the most difficult crops and oats were below average, while oilseed rape did best.

soil_restoration_rules.statement: Legume cover crops fix atmospheric nitrogen and add it to the soil, which can reduce later nitrogen fertiliser needs.
Cover crops protect and improve soil during periods when cropland would otherwise be bare.
Cover crop termination should be planned to prepare the field for the next crop and to manage soil moisture.
Cereal rye is a very winter-hardy non-legume cover crop that takes up leftover soil nitrogen (a catch crop), so it suits a field that already grows a legume.

legumes.note: Crops treated as legumes. If the farm's current crop is on this list, the engine does not suggest adding a legume cover crop.

pulses.note: Pulse (grain legume) crops. Pulses should not follow each other closely, so the 3-year table never holds more than one pulse. Forage legumes such as alfalfa and clover are legumes but not pulses.

rule.statement: Leave at least five years between pulse crops, to reduce rotational risks such as soil-borne diseases.

pulses.break_cereal_note: Cereal put in year 3 after a pulse. Both come from the zone's crop rules (winter wheat from CL-1, sorghum from WE-1).

crop_aliases.note: Names treated as the same crop, so a farm is not told to switch to the crop it already grows.

perennials.note: Perennial crops: one stand is kept for several years, so the 3-year table shows planning slots, not a new sowing each year.

rule.statement: Alfalfa is a perennial: one stand can stay productive for four to ten years or more. Reseeding alfalfa straight after alfalfa is not recommended (autotoxicity, seedling disease, pests); a break of at least 12 months has worked.
